title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: "take care." "love, Mom." a sign-off said over and over can still mean everything. hymns in the Rig Veda's seventh book share one
carry: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna, called in pairs: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, joined in one word. Did you find an ampersand and say thank you? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

Take care. Drive safe. Love, Mom. Text me when you get home. Some goodbyes get said so often they're worn smooth, like a step everyone uses. Nobody writes a new one each time. And still, if the person who always says drive safe forgets to say it one day, it's noticed. A sign-off that sounds routine can be carrying the whole relationship. The Rig Veda has one. In its seventh book, the hymns credited to the seer Vasishtha's family, a single closing line returns at the end of hymn after hymn. Hymns to Agni, to Indra, to Ushas, to Varuna. Today, the last day on these hymns: how they say goodbye.
screen: `TAKE CARE. DRIVE SAFE. LOVE, MOM.` → `WORN SMOOTH, STILL MEANT.` → `HOW THE HYMNS SAY GOODBYE.`

segments.voice: The line is: yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. In plain English: you, protect us always with blessings. Svasti is well-being, things going well. Pata means protect, keep. Sada, always. Nah, us. Now listen to the first word. Yuyam. It's you, but plural. You all. Even when a hymn has spent its whole length praising one god, the dawn, say, or the fire, the last line can turn and speak to the gods together. Thank you, Agni, for this morning. And all of you: keep us well. That's a wide goodbye. The hymn to Varuna we heard two days ago, the one where the singer asks what he did wrong, closes this way too. After all that worry, the ending is the same steady line as the hymns of praise. Whatever happened in the middle, the sign-off doesn't change. There's something to that. A refrain isn't lazy writing. It's a promise of return. The singer says it at the end of the dawn hymn, and again at the end of the fire hymn, and the repeating is part of the meaning. Keep us well, always, the same way we keep coming back. And notice what's asked for. Not victory, not riches. Just svasti, well-being, kept. Each of the four voices has had its day. This is how their hymns close: one ordinary, enormous wish, said to all of them at once.
screen: `YUYAM PATA SVASTIBHIH SADA NAH.` · `YUYAM: YOU, PLURAL. ALL OF YOU.` · `THE SAME LINE, AFTER PRAISE OR WORRY.` · `SVASTI: WELL-BEING, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a wide goodbye. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind the people you'll see or talk to today, one at a time. A face, a name. With each, on the out-breath, wish them one plain thing: be well. Then widen it, the way yuyam does. Not just one person but all of them together, and the people they love, and the ones you won't meet. Be well, all of you. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the closing line of hymns in the seventh book: you all, protect us always with well-being. Today's word.
Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, mean your goodbye. When you say take care, slow down and let it carry something. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

fork.setup: you're a singer in Vasishtha's family. you've just finished a hymn to the dawn. how do you close it?
options: a new ending, written just for her
turn to all the gods: protect us always with well-being
fork.reveal: the same line closes hymn after hymn in book seven: yuyam pata svastibhih sada nah. you all, protect us always with well-being.

original.note: Sanskrit: well-being, things going well. In the closing line of hymns in Rig Veda book seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn ends where its praise ends.
what it means: hymns in book seven close with one shared line, turned to all the gods: protect us always with well-being.
what a scholar hears: yūyaṃ pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ, the Vasiṣṭha refrain; yūyam is second-person plural, so even a hymn to one god ends by addressing many.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

notes: Refrain yūyaṃ pāta svastibhiḥ sadā naḥ: confirm it closes hymns in Rig Veda book 7 to Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna (e.g. 7.1, 7.20, 7.77, 7.86); 'hymn after hymn' is used instead of a count.
Confirm that Rig Veda 7.86 (the Varuna hymn of day 1271, written by another writer) ends with this refrain; if not, cut the sentence linking the two.
Glosses: yūyam 'you (plural)', pāta 'protect', svastibhiḥ 'with blessings / well-being', sadā 'always', naḥ 'us'; confirm.
'Not victory, not riches, though other verses ask for those' is a general statement about Vedic requests; confirm or trim.
Svasti glossed without etymology on purpose. Devanagari स्वस्ति; confirm.
